title: Winter Dreams
subtitle: A story by F. Scott Fitzgerald (1922) — a poor boy, a rich girl, and a dream that comes true.
crosslink: Want the fuller version? Read this story at B2/C1 level →
grammar_tab: Grammar — want to / would like to / hope to
intention: you'll tell the story of a boy who wants everything and gets it, and use want to, would like to and hope to to talk about dreams and plans.
warmup: What did you want to be when you were fourteen? Did it happen?
Is money the most important thing for a happy life? What is?
Have you ever wanted something very much and then, when you got it, felt nothing?
vocab_intro: Before we read, let's learn the words you'll need. Think first — then click Reveal to check.

vocab.heading: A. Guess from the sentence
vocab.instruction: Read the sentence. What does the bold word mean? Then reveal.

items.sent: A caddy carries the golf clubs for a rich player and finds the ball when it is lost. Dexter was the best caddy in the club.
items.meaning: a caddy (n) — a person who carries a golfer's clubs.

items.sent: In summer the rich people played golf on the green course by the lake. They hit a small white ball with a long club.
items.meaning: golf (n) — a game where you hit a small ball into holes with long clubs.

items.sent: Dexter bought a laundry — a business where clothes are washed and cleaned for other people. Soon he had five of them.
items.meaning: a laundry (n) — a business that washes clothes for customers.

items.sent: Dexter and Irene were engaged. The wedding was going to be in September.
items.meaning: engaged (adj) — having promised to marry someone. to get engaged

vocab.heading: B. Which word is it?
vocab.instruction: Read the meaning. Say the word. The first letter helps you.

items.sent: Having a lot of money. It begins with r.
items.meaning: rich (adj). The rich people from the island played golf.

items.sent: A big hope for the future — something you want very much. It begins with d.
items.meaning: a dream (n) / to dream (v). His winter dreams were about being rich.

items.sent: Very pleasing to look at — the opposite of ugly. It begins with b.
items.meaning: beautiful (adj). Judy Jones was the most beautiful girl on the lake.

vocab.heading: C. Choose the meaning
vocab.instruction: Read the sentence and choose a, b or c. Then reveal.

items.sent: Judy began to cry quietly in the car. — to cry means: (a) to laugh (b) to have tears come from your eyes (c) to shout
items.meaning: (b) — to cry (v) — to have tears come from your eyes because you are sad.

items.sent: Seven years later, Judy was married and had children. — married means: (a) very rich (b) living alone (c) having a husband or wife
items.meaning: (c) — married (adj) — having a husband or wife. to get married

items.sent: "The dream is gone," he thought. "I have lost something, and it will never come back." — to lose means: (a) to find (b) to no longer have something (c) to buy
items.meaning: (b) — to lose (v) — to no longer have something. lose – lost – lost

Look at the ten words. Is this a happy story? Guess how it ends.
story_intro: This is a famous American story, told here in simple English. Read each part, then try the questions from memory.

story.title: Part 1 — The boy who quit
paras: Dexter Green is fourteen. He lives in a small town in Minnesota, by a lake. In summer he works as a caddy at the golf club: he carries the rich men's golf clubs. He is the best caddy in the club. He never loses a ball.

In winter, the golf course is under snow. Dexter skis over it and dreams. He dreams that he is a golf champion. He dreams that he is rich, with a big car, and everybody looks at him. These are his winter dreams.

One morning a little girl comes to the club: Judy Jones, eleven years old. She is with her nurse, and she has five new golf clubs. She is not pretty yet — but she will be, and everybody can see it. "Boy!" she says to Dexter. "Do you know where the golf teacher is?" Then she has an argument with her nurse and hits her golf club on the ground, very hard.

Dexter watches her. Something happens inside him. When the caddy-master says, "Go and carry the young lady's clubs," Dexter says: "No. I'm quitting. I'm too old." He gives back his badge and walks home. He does not want to be a caddy for Judy Jones. His winter dreams have decided.

check.q: What is Dexter's job, and what does he dream about in winter?
check.a: He is a caddy at the golf club. In winter he dreams that he is a golf champion and a rich man.
A rich little girl, Judy Jones, calls him 'Boy' and wants a caddy. Something happens inside him — he does not want to carry her clubs. He quits.

story.discuss: Dexter gives up the best job on the lake because of an eleven-year-old girl. Why? What does it tell you about him?

story.title: Part 2 — Judy Jones
paras: Dexter goes to a famous university in the East. Then he starts a business: a laundry. He learns to wash rich men's golf socks perfectly. Soon he has five laundries. At twenty-three, he is making more money than any young man in the state.

One weekend, a rich man invites him to play golf at the same club where he was a caddy. Now he is a guest. On the course, a golf ball flies over a hill and hits one of the men in the stomach. A girl comes over the hill. "Sorry! I shouted 'Fore!'" It is Judy Jones. She is twenty now, and she is beautiful.

That night Dexter swims out to a raft in the lake. A motor-boat comes roaring across the water. Judy is driving it. "Can you drive a boat? Then drive this one, and I'll surf behind. My name is Judy Jones." He drives. She stands on the surf-board with her arms wide open. "Why don't you come to dinner tomorrow night?"

At dinner, her parents are not there. After dinner she says: "Do you mind if I cry a little? A man I liked told me today that he is poor. I didn't know. Let's start right — who are you?" "I'm nobody," says Dexter. "Are you poor?" "No. I'm probably making more money than any man my age." She smiles, and moves closer, and kisses him. Dexter knows now: he has wanted Judy Jones since he was a little boy.

check.a: He starts a laundry business and learns to wash rich men's golf socks perfectly. Soon he has five laundries.

check.q: What does Judy ask Dexter after dinner?
check.a: 'Who are you?' and 'Are you poor?' He says he is nobody, but he is not poor — he makes more money than any man his age.

story.discuss: 'Are you poor?' — 'No.' — and then she kisses him. What is Judy really asking?

story.title: Part 3 — The dream is gone
paras: For two years, Dexter loves Judy Jones. It is terrible. One week she loves him; the next week she goes away with another man. She has a dozen men around her. She says "kiss me", she says "I'd like to marry you" — and she means nothing. She is bored with everybody.
At last Dexter gives up. He gets engaged to a nice girl called Irene. Irene is kind and honest and a little fat. The wedding will be in September. Dexter is calm. He is not happy, but he is calm.

Then, one night in May, Judy comes back. She walks across the dance floor in a gold dress. "Hello, darling. Have you got a car?" In the car she says: "I'm tired of everything, Dexter. I wish you'd marry me." He should tell her about Irene. He cannot. Judy starts to cry. "I'm more beautiful than anybody. Why can't I be happy? Won't you come in?" "All right," he says. "I'll come in."
Judy loves him for one month. Then it is over. Dexter has lost Irene, and he has not got Judy. He goes to the war, and then to New York, and becomes very rich.

Seven years later, a man from Detroit comes to Dexter's office. "You're from the Middle West? A friend of mine married a girl from your town. Judy Jones. Her husband drinks. She stays home with the kids. She was a pretty girl once." "Once?" says Dexter. "She was the most beautiful girl in the world!" "Oh, she's all right," says the man. "She has nice eyes."

When the man goes, Dexter lies down and looks out at the New York sky. He tries to see Judy's face, the lake, the moon. He cannot. The dream is gone. For the first time in years, he cries — but only for himself. "Long ago," he says, "there was something in me. Now it is gone. I cannot cry. I cannot care. It will never come back."

check.q: What does Dexter do when Judy comes back in May?
check.a: He forgets Irene and goes with Judy. Judy loves him for one month, and then it is over. He loses both of them.

check.q: What does the man from Detroit tell him seven years later?
check.a: That Judy is married to a man who drinks, she stays home with the children, and she is not beautiful any more — 'she's all right'.

story.discuss: Dexter is rich. He has everything he dreamed of. Why does he cry?

grammar.h2: The grammar this story runs on: wanting and hoping
grammar.intro: This is a story about wanting. Dexter wants to be rich; Judy would like to marry him (this week); Irene hopes to be happy. Three verbs, one small rule: they are all followed by to + verb.
notes:
want to + verb — a strong wish.
• "I want to be rich." • "He doesn't want to be a caddy." • "What do you want to do?"

would like to + verb — a polite wish or offer.
• "I'd like to marry you." • "Would you like to come to dinner?" — "Yes, I'd love to."
• Short form: I'd, you'd, she'd = would.

hope to + verb — a wish for the future that may or may not happen.
• "She hopes to be happy." • "I hope to see you again."
Careful: after these verbs, always to + base verb: ✗ want be, ✗ would like marry. ✓ want to be, would like to marry.

exercises.instruction: Complete with want to, wants to, doesn't want to or wanted to.
items: At fourteen, Dexter ___ be a golf champion.
He ___ carry Judy's golf clubs, so he quits.
Now he ___ be rich — and he is.
"What do you ___ do with your life?" his father asks.

exercises.h3: would like to — polite wishes and offers
exercises.instruction: Make the sentence or question with would like to.
items: "___ (you / come) to dinner tomorrow night?" — "Yes, I'd love to."
Dexter ___ (take) Judy with him to New York.

At fourteen, he ___ be a champion one day.
"I ___ see you again," says the man from Detroit.

grammar.outro: In the Speak tab, say what each person in the story wants to do, would like to do, and hopes to do — and what really happens.

deeper.h2: Why people still read this story
paras: F. Scott Fitzgerald (1896–1940) wrote this story in 1922, when he was twenty-six. Three years later he used the same idea for his famous novel The Great Gatsby: a poor boy, a rich girl, money, and a dream. The lake in the story is real — Fitzgerald spent his summers there.

Dexter gets everything he wants. He is rich. He is successful. Nobody can stop him. But the dream was never really about money — it was about wanting. When the man says Judy is 'all right', Dexter learns that the beautiful thing he wanted has gone — and, worse, that he cannot feel anything about it any more.
deeper.note: Look at the beginning again. Dexter quits the best job on the lake the first time he sees Judy. Fifteen years later he leaves Irene the first night Judy comes back. Is it the same thing?
questions: Is Judy Jones a bad person? Or is she just beautiful and bored?
Irene is kind and honest. Why can't Dexter love her?
Dexter is rich at the end. Is he happy? Is being rich enough?
Would you like to be Dexter at fourteen, or Dexter at thirty-two?

speak.intro: This is the heart of the lesson — do all three out loud. The timer helps you keep going: fill the time with details.
speak.useful: Wishes and plans: "He wants to…", "She would like to…", "They hope to…" What really happens: "But in fact…", "In the end…" For opinions: "I think…", "In my opinion…", "The sad thing is…".

tasks.label: Task A · Tell the story (4 minutes)
paras: Tell 'Winter Dreams' to someone who does not know it: the caddy and the winter → Judy at eleven → the laundries → the boat → dinner → two terrible years → Irene → the gold dress → seven years later.
Use want to / would like to / hope to, and at least five key words (caddy, golf, laundry, engaged, rich, dream, beautiful, cry, married, lose).

tasks.label: Task B · Is Judy bad? (3 minutes)
paras: Some readers hate Judy Jones. Do you? Give your opinion and two reasons. Then say the opposite for one minute.

tasks.label: Task C · Dreams (4 minutes)
paras: Talk about dreams and plans — yours, or someone else's. Use want to, would like to and hope to.
menu: What you wanted to be at fourteen — and what happened.
A famous person who got their dream and was not happy.
Three things you would like to do in the next five years.
A character in a film who wants something too much.
What your parents hoped for you — and what you hoped for yourself.
A story you invent: a poor boy, a rich girl, and one wish.

final: Dexter cries 'only for himself'. Is that sad, or honest?
Would you quit your job for a dream? Did Dexter do the right thing at fourteen?
Is there something you want so much that you are afraid to get it?
Before you go — from memory: three sentences — one with want to, one with would like to, one with hope to — about three different people in the story.
